title: The hidden life (CCC 531–534)
hookLine: most of Jesus's life was ordinary work in Nazareth

cards: "Is not this the carpenter, the son of Mary?" That's the hometown crowd in Mark's Gospel, and they aren't impressed.
Jesus has come back to his own country, teaching in the synagogue, and the people who watched him grow up can't square it. They know his mother. They know his brothers by name.
They know him as the carpenter. Their question is accidentally a window. Before the crowds and the miracles, there were years so ordinary that the neighbors remembered him mostly as a tradesman.
The Catechism has a name for those years.

teach.b: For the greater part of his life, the Catechism says, Jesus shared the condition of the vast majority of people: a daily life without evident greatness, manual work, the religious life of his people, life in a community.
The Gospels are nearly silent about them. The one event that breaks the silence, the Catechism says, is the finding in the temple.
When Jesus was twelve, Luke tells, his family went up to Jerusalem for the feast, and on the way home his parents realized he wasn't with them.
After three days they found him in the temple, among the teachers, listening and asking questions. Then a line closes the door on the hidden years again.
In the Douay-Rheims: "And he went down with them, and came to Nazareth, and was subject to them." Luke adds one more sentence: "And Jesus advanced in wisdom, and age, and grace with God and men."
Back to the workshop, the family table, the synagogue on the sabbath. The Catechism sees in his obedience to Mary and Joseph a picture of his obedience to the Father.
And because of Nazareth, it says, anyone can share in Jesus's life through the most ordinary events of their own day.

teach.h: A SCHOOL OF SILENCE, FAMILY, WORK.
teach.b: It quotes Pope Paul the Sixth, speaking at Nazareth, who called it a school: a lesson in silence, in family life, in work. So the plain parts of a life aren't a waiting room before the real thing starts.
In Catholic teaching, God made flesh spent most of his years on them.

how: Catholics honor the hidden life at Nazareth on the feast of the Holy Family and in the rosary's joyful mysteries, which end with the finding of Jesus in the temple.

practice: Bring to mind the plainest job waiting for you today, dishes, emails, a diaper, a shift, a form, and don't try to make it meaningful.
Just see yourself doing it carefully, as if the person it serves were in the room, and notice your hands and the pace you'd like to go at.
If you pray, offer that one task to God before you start; if you don't, simply choose the person you're doing it for.
